title: Never Put Too Much Trust in Friends, Learn How to Use Enemies
coreMove: Replace sentimental trust with incentive clarity when power puts loyalty under strain
sourcePressure: why friendship can blur incentives, why former enemies can behave more predictably under pressure, and where that argument becomes too cynical.

sourceAnchors.name: Michael III
sourceAnchors.detail: elevated Basilius and was later overthrown by him
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Michael III trusted the emotional comfort of friendship and missed the appetite growing beside him.

sourceAnchors.name: Basilius
sourceAnchors.detail: the trusted friend whose rise under Michael III turned into betrayal
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Basilius is the warning that affection can hide entitlement until power gives it a door.

sourceAnchors.name: Talleyrand and Fouche
sourceAnchors.detail: former enemies used each other because clear incentives made the alliance more legible than friendship
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Talleyrand and Fouche worked from the clarity of mutual caution, not the fog of sentiment.
